The work, with numbers attached.

### Card 1

**Metric (card headline):**
2–4 proposals a day, 15 minutes each.

**Client:** Dahlia+ Agency — event production, team of six to eight.

**Mechanism:**
An accepted proposal in Fresh Proposals updates the HubSpot deal stage, builds the Monday.com board, and creates the QuickBooks customer with two 50/50 invoices — untouched. At 2–4 proposals a day, that's 6–8 hours of manual operations gone from every working day.

Read the Dahlia+ case study →

### Card 2

**Metric (card headline):**
400+ articles a day. Ten make the newsletter.

**Client:** Matador Network — travel media, editorial team of twelve.

**Mechanism:**
Overnight, an AI reads eleven-plus publications, picks the ten stories that matter, and delivers a finished newsletter every morning. Their creator tracker went from 5 hours a week to 1.5 — covering 70 creators instead of 30.

Read the Matador case study →

### Card 3

**Metric (card headline):**
From zero operational visibility to automated daily reporting.

**Client:** TPS Workforce Hub — clean-tech workforce training, Boston. 30–40 applicants per cohort.

**Mechanism:**
Six connected systems run their admissions and operations — AI-scored interviews from Read.ai transcripts, scheduling, stipend-eligibility alerts, and the 5pm report the whole team reads.

How an engagement works

### Step 1 — Discovery call. 60 minutes.

You walk me through how the work actually happens, and I look for where the hours go. Book it directly on my calendar.

### Step 2 — Solution design. A few days.

You get a written scope: what I'll build, what it connects to, the fixed price, and the timeline. Nothing starts until you've approved it.

### Step 3 — Build and test. One to four weeks.

I build on your systems and test against your real data, checking in as each piece goes live.

### Step 4 — Handoff. One call.

You get documentation and a recorded walkthrough of everything I built.

### Ownership statement:

You own all of it. The workflows run in your accounts under your credentials — if we ever part ways, everything keeps running.

### What "embedded" means:

Most clients keep me on after handoff, working inside their Slack, their CRM, their boards — a team member who happens to be an automation engineer. That's how one automation at Dahlia+ became four, and one system at TPS Workforce Hub became six.

Questions I get on every discovery call

**What a custom build costs**
Builds start at $1,500, with a fixed price set in writing after the discovery call. If you start with the $500 audit, that full amount is credited toward the build.

**How long a build takes**
One to four weeks for most projects, depending on how many systems are involved. The timeline is in the scope document before work begins.

**Who does the actual work**
I do — every workflow, every integration, every fix. pocho.tech is one engineer, and you work with me directly from the first call through handoff.

**Who owns what I build**
You do. Everything runs in your accounts under your credentials, with documentation and a recorded walkthrough at handoff — it all keeps running with or without me.

**What happens after handoff**
Most clients keep me on. All three teams on this page started with a single build and continue on embedded retainers, scoped per engagement.

**The tools I can connect**
The twelve automations in production span more than twenty tools — HubSpot, Airtable, Monday.com, QuickBooks, Slack, Supabase, SharePoint, Power Automate, Apify, Google Analytics 4, Gmail, and others. If your tool has an API, it can probably join the list; the discovery call settles it.

**Templates versus custom builds**
Buy a template when the workflow matches your stack as described — it's the same kind of system, with Done-For-You Setup available for $100. Commission a build when the process is specific to how your team works.

**Where to start**
If you know what you want built, book the discovery call. If you don't, the $500 audit gives you a written plan within five business days — credited in full if you go ahead.

Three teams run twelve of my automations in production. Every one of those engagements started on one of the rungs below.

## How the options compare

| | Working with pocho.tech | Hiring an ops person | Doing it yourself on Zapier |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cost** | From $1,500 per build, fixed in writing; retainers scoped per engagement | A full-time salary, plus recruiting and ramp-up | The subscription, plus your own hours |
| **Time to a working system** | One to four weeks from approved scope | Months before the first build ships | Fast for a two-step trigger; slow for multi-system pipelines with AI steps |
| **Who does the work** | One engineer with twelve automations in production | A generalist whose week includes much more than automation | You, between everything else on your plate |
| **What you keep** | Workflows in your accounts, documented, with a recorded walkthrough | Institutional knowledge that leaves with the employee | Workflows only you understand |

If a simple Zapier trigger genuinely covers your case, you'll hear that on the discovery call.

# Automation Audit

The audit is a 60-minute review of how your team actually works, followed by a written report within five business days. It costs $500, credited in full toward a custom build — if you go ahead, the plan cost you nothing.

You leave with priorities, tools, estimated time savings, and a build scope for every recommendation.

[Book an audit](https://calendly.com/erick-pocho/1hr-session)

---

## What the report contains

Four things, specific to your team and your tools:

- **What to automate first** — your workflows ranked by hours recovered against effort to build
- **The tools for each** — which platforms and APIs every recommendation would connect
- **Estimated time savings** — what each automation should give back, per week
- **A build scope per recommendation** — what it would cost and roughly how long it would take

Whether you build with me, build in-house, or shelve it for a quarter, you have the plan in writing.

## How it works

**The call — 60 minutes.** You walk me through how the work actually happens, ideally with the person who does it day to day on the call. [Book it directly on my calendar](https://calendly.com/erick-pocho/1hr-session).

**The report — within five business days.** A written document covering the four sections above, specific to your tools and your volume.

## Why start here

A custom build is $1,500 or more, and the right first automation isn't always obvious from inside the team. The audit answers that in writing before you commit to anything.

If you commission a build afterward, the full $500 comes off the price. If you don't, you keep a plan any competent engineer could execute.

Sometimes the report says a $249 template covers it, or that a workflow isn't worth automating yet. You get that in writing too.

---

## Questions before you book an audit

### How the $500 credit works

Commission a custom build after the audit and the full $500 comes off that build's price. Builds start at $1,500, so the audit effectively becomes a deposit on the work.

### What I need from you

Sixty minutes with whoever actually does the work, and honest answers about how it happens today — including the spreadsheet workarounds. The closer I get to the real process, the sharper the report.

### What happens if there's little worth automating

That goes in the report. If the right answer is a $249 template, a process change, or no automation at all, the report says so.

# Custom Automation Build

A custom automation build at pocho.tech starts at $1,500, with a fixed price set in writing after a 60-minute discovery call. I design the workflow, build and test it on your systems, and hand it off with documentation and a recorded walkthrough — typically in one to four weeks.

I'm Erick Bonilla, and I'm the engineer on every build — first call through handoff.

[Book a discovery call](https://calendly.com/erick-pocho/1hr-session)

---

## What a custom build looks like

The clearest example runs at Dahlia+ Agency, an event production company with a team of six to eight.

When a proposal is accepted in Fresh Proposals, the automation updates the HubSpot deal stage, builds the Monday.com board, and creates the QuickBooks customer with two invoices split 50/50 — untouched by anyone. Processing one proposal went from 1.5–2 hours to 15 minutes.

At 2–4 proposals a day, that's 6–8 hours of manual operations gone from every working day.

Other builds running in production:

- **AI interview evaluation — TPS Workforce Hub.** Read.ai interview transcripts arrive by webhook; candidates get matched and objectively scored, and human reviewers get a structured brief with direct quotes from the interview.
- **AI newsletter curator — Matador Network.** Overnight, an AI reads 400+ articles across eleven-plus publications, picks the top ten, and delivers a finished newsletter every morning with zero human input.
- **Business card scanner — Dahlia+ Agency.** Drop a photo in Slack; GPT-4o Vision reads the card, extracts every field, and creates the HubSpot contact.

## What it costs

Builds start at $1,500. The price depends on how many systems the workflow touches, the volume moving through it, and whether AI evaluation or parsing needs design and testing of its own.

You get the fixed number in writing in the scope document, before any work begins. If you started with the [$500 audit](/services/automation-audit), that full amount comes off the price.

## How the process works

**1. Discovery call — 60 minutes.** You walk me through how the work actually happens, and I look for where the hours go. [Book it directly on my calendar](https://calendly.com/erick-pocho/1hr-session).

**2. Solution design — a few days.** You get a written scope: what I'll build, what it connects to, the fixed price, and the timeline. Nothing starts until you've approved it.

**3. Build and test — one to four weeks.** I build on your systems and test against your real data, checking in as each piece goes live.

**4. Handoff — one call.** You get documentation and a recorded walkthrough of everything I built.

## Who owns what I build

You do. The workflows run in your accounts under your credentials — if we ever part ways, everything keeps running.

There is no platform of mine in the middle and no ongoing fee back to me for what you own.

## What happens after handoff

Most clients keep me on. All three teams on this site started with a single build and continue on embedded retainers, scoped per engagement.

> "Erick was incredibly helpful in setting up the system to automatically track creator content. This automation saves me roughly 3-4 hours per week, and has made my workflow much smoother and saves a lot of manual effort."
> — Kyrene Kagahastian, Social Media Team, Matador Network

---

## Questions I get before a build starts

### What determines the price

The number of systems involved, the volume moving through the workflow, and whether AI steps need their own design and testing. The Dahlia+ pipeline touches four systems; a workflow that touches one costs less to build.

### How long a build takes

One to four weeks for most projects, depending on how many systems are involved. The timeline is in the scope document before work begins.

### Who maintains it after handoff

Either your team, using the documentation and recorded walkthrough, or me, on a retainer scoped per engagement. When something breaks, you message the person who wrote it.

### Which tools I can connect

The twelve automations in production span more than twenty tools — HubSpot, Airtable, Monday.com, QuickBooks, Slack, Supabase, SharePoint, Power Automate, Apify, Google Analytics 4, Gmail, and others. If your tool has an API, it can probably join the list; the discovery call settles it.

# Done-For-You Setup

Done-For-You Setup adds $100 to any template in the catalog. We meet on a live 60–90 minute call: I connect your credentials, configure the workflow for your accounts, and test it with you watching — and you keep a recording of the whole session.

You buy the workflow; I make sure it's running before we hang up.

[Browse the templates](/templates)

---

## How the session works

**Before the call.** You buy the template, add the setup option, and book a time on my calendar. I send a short list of the logins and access the workflow needs, so the session starts at full speed.

**On the call — 60 to 90 minutes.** I connect each credential, configure the workflow for your accounts, and run it live until it behaves on your real data. Then I walk you through how it works and where to adjust it.

**After the call.** The workflow is live in your accounts, and the recording arrives so anyone on your team can replay the entire setup.

## What you walk away with

- The workflow running in your accounts, under your credentials
- A recording of the full session
- The template's step-by-step PDF guide and 90-second walkthrough video
- Working knowledge of where to change it when your process changes

## Which templates this covers

All seven, including the free Sheets ↔ HubSpot sync. Jarvis — the AI executive assistant — is the most involved template in the catalog, which makes it the one where the setup session earns its $100 most clearly.

[Browse the templates](/templates)

---

## Questions before you book a session

### What I need from you before the call

Admin access to the tools the template connects — for the Business Card Scanner, that's Slack, OpenAI, and HubSpot. The exact list for your template is in its PDF guide, and I send it again when you book.

### Whether you could set it up yourself instead

Yes — every template ships with the workflow JSON, a step-by-step PDF, and a walkthrough video, and most go live in under an hour on your own. The session is for teams that want it running today, verified live on their data, with a recording to keep.

### What happens if the template doesn't match your stack

Each template works as described with the tools listed on its page. If your stack is different — another CRM, extra steps in the process — that's a [custom build](/services/custom-automation) conversation, and you can write to me first at [erick.bonilla63@gmail.com](mailto:erick.bonilla63@gmail.com) to check before buying.

# n8n & Make.com Consulting

I consult on n8n and Make.com: architecture review, workflow builds, self-hosting guidance, and team training. I'm Erick Bonilla — the twelve automations I run in production for Dahlia+ Agency, Matador Network, and TPS Workforce Hub are built on these platforms with the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs.

Engagements are scoped on a discovery call.

[Book a discovery call](https://calendly.com/erick-pocho/1hr-session)

---

## The shortest version of my credentials

Matador Network brought me in to teach n8n to their AI Advocacy Director. The training led to a hire: their editorial team now runs four of my automations, including a newsletter curator that processes 400+ articles a day.

> "Erick has helped us build and implement multiple automations for our editorial department, and these save us time each week that can be spent producing content rather than sifting through emails and data."
> — Tim Wenger, Editorial Team, Matador Network

## What consulting covers

### Architecture review

I read your existing workflows and tell you what will break first — error handling, credential management, rate limits, and the nodes doing too much work. You get specific fixes, in writing.

### Workflow builds

Some teams bring a half-built workflow; some bring a blank canvas. Either way I build on your instance, alongside your team, so the knowledge stays when the engagement ends.

### Self-hosting guidance

Whether to self-host n8n or stay on cloud, and how to run it if you do: environments, credentials, backups, and upgrades. The goal is an instance your team can operate without me.

### Team training

The same thing Matador Network hired me for first: teaching your team to build and maintain workflows in-house. Sessions are scoped to your stack and the workflows you actually need.

## How engagements are scoped

On a discovery call. Some engagements are a single architecture-review session; some become standing arrangements, scoped per engagement like all my retainer work.

If what you actually need is a finished system rather than guidance, that's a [custom build](/services/custom-automation) — from $1,500.

---

## Questions teams ask before a consulting engagement

### n8n vs Zapier vs Make — which to use

Zapier is the fastest start for simple triggers; Make.com handles longer visual scenarios at moderate cost; n8n gives the most control — self-hostable, with code where you need it, and well suited to AI-heavy workflows. I build client systems on both n8n and Make.com, so the recommendation isn't a pitch for either platform.

The honest answer depends on your volume, your data constraints, and who maintains it after I leave. It's the first ten minutes of the call.

### Whether I review existing workflows or only build new ones

Both. Architecture review of what you already have is a common starting point — most teams arrive with something half-working rather than a blank slate.

### Self-hosted n8n versus n8n cloud

Cloud is the right default while you're proving that workflows matter to the business. Self-hosting earns its overhead when volume, cost, or data control demand it — and if you go that way, the setup is part of what I cover.

### What consulting costs

Scoped per engagement on the discovery call — a single review session is priced differently than ongoing training. If the engagement turns into me building the system, [builds start at $1,500](/services/custom-automation).

# Dahlia+ Agency

**Event production and consulting — [dahliaplus.com](https://dahliaplus.com).** Team of six to eight, led by Dahlia El Gazzar. Four automations in production, on an embedded retainer.

---

## The before

An accepted proposal set off the same manual relay every time: update the deal in HubSpot, build the project board in Monday.com, create the customer in QuickBooks, draft two invoices, split 50/50. Done by hand, it took an hour and a half to two hours.

At two to four proposals a day, that relay was most of someone's day. Six to eight hours of manual operations, every working day, inside a team of six to eight people.

Leads had the same shape at smaller scale. Web form submissions, referrals arriving by email, business cards collected at events — each one re-typed into HubSpot, or lost on the way there.

---

## What I built

Four automations run the Dahlia+ back office.

1. **Proposal-to-invoice pipeline** — An accepted proposal in Fresh Proposals updates the HubSpot deal stage, builds the Monday.com board, and creates the QuickBooks customer with two invoices split 50/50.
2. **Web form lead routing** — Every form submission creates the HubSpot contact, adds the subscriber in Beehiiv, and posts to Slack so the team sees the lead the moment it arrives.
3. **AI referral capture** — An AI parses referral emails as they land and creates the contact in HubSpot, so an introduction doesn't depend on someone remembering to copy it over.
4. **Business card scanner** — Drop a photo in Slack; GPT-4o Vision reads the card, extracts every field, and creates the HubSpot contact.

---

## The numbers

**1.5–2 hours → 15 minutes**
Processing one proposal, accepted to invoiced.

**2–4 a day**
Proposals through the pipeline.

**6–8 hours**
Manual operations eliminated from every working day.

---

## The stack

HubSpot, Monday.com, QuickBooks, Slack, Gmail, Beehiiv, Fresh Proposals, OpenAI GPT-4o Vision.

---

## On testimonials

No testimonial exists for this engagement, so none appears here. What does exist: Dahlia+ now refers new business.

---

## How it started

One automation, scoped on a discovery call. Working embedded, one became four — and the retainer is still running.

# TPS Workforce Hub

**Clean-tech workforce training — Boston.** The EdTech division of TPS Energy runs an 8-week, stipend-based training program for immigrants and minorities. 30–40 applicants per cohort; 12–16 accepted. Six systems in production, built as an embedded team member.

---

## The before

Every cohort starts with 30 to 40 applications and ends with 12 to 16 seats. Between those two numbers: intake forms, interviews, scoring, scheduling emails, stipend rules, and a team holding it together by hand.

There was no operational visibility. Nobody could see, in one place, where a candidate stood, which interviews had been evaluated, or who was at risk of losing stipend eligibility.

The stipend part carried the most weight. Eligibility data sat in SharePoint, invisible to the participant and coach who needed the warning.

---

## What I built

Six connected systems, running as one operation.

1. **Airtable ATS** — Intake forms feed one applicant pipeline, so every candidate has a single record and a visible stage from application to acceptance.
2. **AI interview evaluation** — A Read.ai transcript webhook matches the candidate, applies objective scoring, runs an AI qualitative evaluation with direct quotes from the interview, and delivers a structured brief to the human reviewers.
3. **Interview scheduling** — Scheduling emails go out automatically as candidates advance through the pipeline.
4. **Daily and executive reporting** — A 5pm report to the team every day, and a Monday executive summary for the CEO: week-over-week movement, demographics, bottleneck alerts.
5. **Stipend eligibility notifications** — SharePoint data flows through Power Automate into Supabase; every Sunday, at-risk participants and their coach get an alert.
6. **Real-time dashboards** — Live views of the pipeline and program operations.

The AI doesn't decide who gets in. It reads, scores, and prepares the brief — the human reviewers make the call.

---

## The numbers

**Zero → daily**
From zero operational visibility to fully automated daily reporting.

**30–40 → 12–16**
Applicants to accepted, every stage tracked.

**Sunday, every week**
At-risk stipend alerts to participant and coach, before the problem lands.

---

## What the CEO says

> "You have done such a great job that I can't remember how we were working before you."
> — CEO, TPS Energy

---

## The stack

Airtable, OpenAI, Read.ai, Supabase, SendGrid, Microsoft Power Automate, SharePoint, Gmail.

---

## How it started

A single build, then embedded work inside the team — one system became six as each bottleneck surfaced.

---

# Matador Network

**Travel media — [matadornetwork.com](https://matadornetwork.com).** Around 50 people, with an editorial team of twelve. Matador also operates GuideGeek, an AI travel product for destination marketing organizations. Four automations in production.

---

## The before

Creator tracking meant opening TikTok and Instagram, finding every post, and copying URLs, views, and likes into a sheet by hand. Five hours a week covered 30 creators, and the program needed to be larger.

The morning news sweep had the same shape. Eleven-plus industry publications produce roughly 400 articles a day; an editorial team of twelve needed the ten worth reading.

Affiliate reporting and event research rounded it out — more data someone had to go collect before the editorial work could start.

---

## What I built

Four automations run the editorial back office.

1. **Creator tracker** — Scrapes TikTok and Instagram for every tracked creator and delivers a Monday digest of post URLs, views, and likes.
2. **AI newsletter curator** — Apify collects roughly 400 articles a day from eleven-plus publications overnight; GPT-4o picks the top ten, writes the summaries, and a polished HTML newsletter arrives every morning.
3. **Affiliate link performance report** — Every Monday, GA4 data becomes a report ranking the top 20 affiliate links, with AI insights.
4. **Event search** — A monthly sweep of Eventbrite, Meetup, and Luma across 15 US cities.

---

## The numbers

**5 hrs/week → 1.5 hrs**
Creator tracking, by hand versus automated.

**30 → 70**
Creators tracked, same workflow.

**400+ a day**
Articles processed into one newsletter, zero human input.

One more metric that doesn't fit in a stat block: when the tracker goes down, the team emails within hours asking for it back.

# AI Automation for Media & Publishing — pocho.tech

---


400+ articles a day go in. A finished newsletter comes out every morning.

I build AI automations for editorial back offices — newsletter curation, creator tracking, affiliate reporting, and event research. Four of them run in production at Matador Network, a travel media network of about fifty people with an editorial team of twelve.

Every number on this page is theirs.

Book a discovery call → https://calendly.com/erick-pocho/1hr-session
Get the AI Newsletter Curator — $249 → https://checkout.lemonsqueezy.com/buy/1320787

---


An editorial team's week disappears into work that produces no content. Someone reads eleven publications' worth of daily output to find the ten stories worth covering.

Someone scrolls TikTok and Instagram logging creator posts into a spreadsheet — URL, views, likes, one row at a time. At Matador Network that took five hours a week and covered only thirty creators.

Someone pulls affiliate numbers out of GA4 and reformats them for the Monday meeting. Someone searches Eventbrite, Meetup, and Luma city by city for events worth attending.

---


### AI newsletter curator

Overnight, the system pulls roughly 400 articles a day from eleven-plus publications through Apify, and GPT-4o scores them and picks the top ten. A polished HTML newsletter is in the team's inbox every morning — zero human input along the way.

**Tools:** Apify, OpenAI, Gmail

A generalized version is in the template catalog: AI Newsletter Curator, $249 → https://checkout.lemonsqueezy.com/buy/1320787

### Social media creator tracker

The tracker scrapes TikTok and Instagram for each creator's posts and delivers a Monday digest — every URL with views and likes attached. Tracking went from 5 hours a week to 1.5, while coverage grew from 30 creators to 70.

**Tools:** Apify, Google Sheets, Gmail

### Affiliate link performance report

Every Monday, the report ranks the top twenty affiliate links from GA4 and adds AI commentary on what moved. The numbers arrive formatted for the meeting instead of waiting to be pulled.

**Tools:** Google Analytics 4, Google Sheets, OpenAI

### Event search automation

Once a month, the system searches Eventbrite, Meetup, and Luma across fifteen US cities and delivers the results to the team. Nobody opens fifteen browser tabs.

**Tools:** Apify, Google Sheets, Gmail

The mechanisms are source-agnostic — the curator reads whatever publications you give it, and the tracker follows whatever accounts you list. The travel is in the inputs; the system doesn't care what industry the sources cover.

**How the AI decides what's newsworthy**
GPT-4o scores each article against selection criteria set with your editors, and the prompt is yours to read and adjust. The newsletter is finished when it arrives, and your team can still pull a story before send if they want a check in the loop.

**What a build like this costs**
Custom builds start at $1,500, fixed in writing after a discovery call. If the newsletter curator as described matches your need, the template is $249, with Done-For-You Setup for $100 more.

You own everything — the workflows run in your accounts under your credentials. Matador's four automations are a continuing embedded engagement, which is how most clients run it.

# AI Automation for Marketing & Event Agencies — pocho.tech

---


Dahlia+ Agency gets back six to eight hours of operations a day. Four automations do it.

I build automations for agency operations — lead routing, referral capture, proposal-to-invoice pipelines, and reporting. Four of them run in production at Dahlia+ Agency, an event production and consulting firm of six to eight people.

Their proposal processing went from 1.5–2 hours to fifteen minutes.

Book a discovery call → https://calendly.com/erick-pocho/1hr-session
Get the Business Card Scanner — $249 → https://checkout.lemonsqueezy.com/buy/1320724

---


At a small agency, new business arrives from everywhere — web forms, referral emails, business cards collected at events — and someone retypes each one into the CRM. The ones that don't get retyped don't get followed up.

An accepted proposal kicks off an hour and a half of administration: update the deal stage, build the project board, create the customer in QuickBooks, draft the invoices. At Dahlia+ Agency's pace of two to four proposals a day, that was six to eight hours of manual operations every working day.

---


### Proposal-to-invoice pipeline

When a proposal is accepted in Fresh Proposals, the automation updates the HubSpot deal stage, builds the Monday.com board, and creates the QuickBooks customer with two invoices on a 50/50 split — untouched. Processing went from 1.5–2 hours per proposal to fifteen minutes.

**Tools:** Fresh Proposals, HubSpot, Monday.com, QuickBooks

### Web form lead routing

A form submission becomes a HubSpot contact, joins the Beehiiv list, and posts an alert in Slack. Every lead lands in the same place, logged the moment it arrives.

**Tools:** HubSpot, Beehiiv, Slack

### AI referral capture

An AI parses referral emails as they arrive and creates the HubSpot record — introductions get logged the day they happen. The follow-up starts from the CRM instead of from memory.

**Tools:** Gmail, OpenAI, HubSpot

### Business card scanner

Drop a photo in Slack; an AI reads the card, extracts every field, and creates the HubSpot contact. The same workflow running at Dahlia+ is in the template catalog for $249.

**Tools:** Slack, OpenAI GPT-4o Vision, HubSpot

### Reporting (capability line, below the four)

Client and performance reporting is the same kind of build. At Matador Network, a Monday report ranks the top twenty affiliate links from GA4 with AI commentary — the agency version reports on your clients' numbers instead of your own.

---

**Whether this fits marketing and PR agencies or only event production**
The mechanics are the same: leads arrive, proposals get accepted, invoices get created. Dahlia+ is event production; the tools and deal stages change per agency, and the discovery call settles them.

**What the proposal-to-invoice pipeline needs to run**
At Dahlia+ it connects Fresh Proposals, HubSpot, Monday.com, and QuickBooks. If your stack differs, the pipeline gets rebuilt on your tools — what matters is that each system has a workable API.

**What it costs**
Custom builds start at $1,500, fixed in writing after a discovery call. The business card scanner is $249 as a template, with Done-For-You Setup for $100 more.

Most clients keep me on. Dahlia+ started with one automation and now runs four, on a continuing embedded engagement scoped per engagement.

# AI Automation for Destination Marketing Organizations — pocho.tech

---


What I build for tourism boards, and where the proof comes from.

I build AI automations for DMOs — partner tracking, AI email agents, content pipelines, and lead qualification. I also speak at this industry's conferences.

Book a discovery call → https://calendly.com/erick-pocho/1hr-session

---


A DMO's week is full of work that scales with partner count: tracking what member businesses are posting, opening, and hosting. Most of it lives in spreadsheets that are current only on the day someone updates them.

Planner inquiries and visitor leads arrive by form and email, and qualifying them means reading each one. Partner outreach is the same email written over and over, personalized by hand when there's time.

---


### Partner tracking

An automation that watches your partners' channels — social posts, event listings, announcements — and delivers a digest with every URL and its numbers attached. The same mechanism runs in production at Matador Network, where it tracks 70 creators across TikTok and Instagram in 1.5 hours of staff time a week.

**Tools:** Apify, OpenAI, Google Sheets or your CRM

### AI email agents

An AI that drafts partner and planner emails from your CRM history — it reads each relationship's past correspondence and writes the check-in or follow-up in your voice, with a review step if you want one. A generalized version is in the template catalog: AI Relationship Nurturing Engine, $299 → https://checkout.lemonsqueezy.com/buy/1320599

**Tools:** HubSpot or any CRM, OpenAI, Gmail

### Content pipelines

An AI that reads your region's sources overnight — local news, partner feeds, event calendars — and delivers a curated newsletter every morning. The production version of this system processes 400+ articles a day at Matador Network.

**Tools:** Apify, OpenAI, Gmail

### Lead qualification

An automation that takes each inbound lead — planner RFPs, group inquiries, web forms — scores it against your criteria, and creates the CRM record with the score and reasoning attached. I run AI scoring of this kind in production at TPS Workforce Hub, where it turns interview transcripts into structured briefs for human reviewers.

**Tools:** your CRM, OpenAI

# AI Automation for Accounting & CPA Firms — pocho.tech

---


Quarterly tax letters, assembled by automation, reviewed by your firm.

I build automations for accounting and CPA firms — bookkeeping workflows in QuickBooks Online, practice workflows in TaxDome, quarterly tax letters, and the client communications around every deadline. This page describes what I build for firms; the production numbers elsewhere on this site come from the three named clients I've already automated.

Book a discovery call → https://calendly.com/erick-pocho/1hr-session

---


Every quarter, someone assembles tax letters client by client — pulling the numbers, fitting them into the firm's format, checking names against the file. The work is identical across clients, and it still gets done one at a time.

Before every deadline, someone chases documents: the same reminder, personalized by hand, sent to each client who hasn't uploaded. Status questions arrive all week, and each one means opening TaxDome to look.

---


### Quarterly tax-letter workflow

An automation that assembles each client's quarterly letter — data pulled from your books, the letter drafted by AI in your format, queued for a reviewer before anything goes out. The reviewer approves or edits; the system sends and logs.

**Tools:** QuickBooks Online, TaxDome, OpenAI or Anthropic, Gmail

### Document chasing and deadline communications

An automation that watches which clients haven't submitted, drafts each reminder from that client's actual status, and escalates as the deadline approaches. Nothing sends without the review step your firm sets.

**Tools:** TaxDome, Gmail, OpenAI

### Bookkeeping workflows in QuickBooks Online

Automations that create customers and invoices, move data between systems, and keep the books in sync with the tools around them. QuickBooks invoice creation already runs in my production work — the Dahlia+ Agency pipeline creates the customer and two invoices the moment a proposal is accepted.

**Tools:** QuickBooks Online, plus whatever feeds it

### Client intake and status

Intake that creates the client record everywhere it needs to exist, and status updates drafted automatically when work moves stages. The inbox stops being the status system.

**Tools:** TaxDome, Gmail, your CRM

---


No accounting firm is named on this page yet — when one is, the numbers will be here. The component systems are in production elsewhere.

- QuickBooks automation runs daily at Dahlia+ Agency: proposal acceptance to customer plus two invoices, untouched.
- AI drafting with human review runs at TPS Workforce Hub: structured AI evaluations delivered to human reviewers, plus automated daily reporting.
- Twelve automations in production across three teams, spanning more than twenty tools.

---


**Whether I've automated a CPA firm before**
Not one I can name on this page yet, and the page doesn't pretend otherwise. The component systems — QuickBooks automation, AI drafting with review steps, deadline-driven communications — each run in production for the named clients on this site.

**How client financial data is handled**
Everything runs in your accounts under your credentials, and the data stays in your systems. I work under whatever access you grant, and you can revoke it at any time.

**Whether AI sends anything to clients unreviewed**
Only if you decide it should. Default builds queue every AI-drafted letter and email for a reviewer — automation removes the assembly work, and the review step stays.

**Where to start**
The $500 audit fits firms well: a 60-minute review of one workflow — quarterly letters are a common pick — then a written report within five business days. Credited in full toward a build.

# Who I am and how I work

I'm Erick Bonilla — founder and the only engineer at pocho.tech. Every workflow on this site I scoped and built myself, and most of them I still operate.

pocho.tech is the AI automation studio of Erick Bonilla. He designs and builds custom AI-powered automations for small teams — event agencies, media companies, tourism organizations, and accounting firms — working embedded inside each client's tools and team.

That's the formal version. The practical version: you tell me where your team's hours go, and I build the system that gets them back.

## What embedded looks like, week to week

Most engagements don't end at handoff — the three client teams on this site all kept me on after the first build. Here is what an ordinary week looks like.

**I'm in your Slack.** Requests, fixes, and ideas happen in the channels where your team already works.

**I work inside your accounts.** Workflows run on your systems under your credentials; when I build or fix something, it happens where you can see it.

**We have a standing touchpoint.** A weekly check-in covers what shipped, what broke, and what's worth building next.

That rhythm is how one automation at Dahlia+ became four, and one system at TPS Workforce Hub became six.

## The three teams

- **Dahlia+ Agency** (event production, team of six to eight) — four automations, including the proposal-to-invoice pipeline that cut processing from 1.5–2 hours to 15 minutes.
- **Matador Network** (travel media, editorial team of twelve) — four automations, including a newsletter curator that reads 400+ articles a day and a creator tracker covering 70 creators.
- **TPS Workforce Hub** (clean-tech workforce training, Boston) — six connected systems running admissions and operations, from AI-scored interviews to the 5pm report the whole team reads.

## What I build with

I build on n8n and Make.com, with the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs handling the reasoning. Across twelve automations in production, that stack connects more than twenty tools — HubSpot, Airtable, Monday.com, QuickBooks, Slack, Supabase, Apify, Google Analytics 4, and others.

I also speak about this work at industry conferences. Matador Network hired me to build after I taught n8n to their AI Advocacy Director — teaching the tools and building with them are the same job to me.

## The name

Pocho is what my family has always called me.
